lessons.title: Letterform and Readability
lessons.essential: How do type anatomy, spacing and contrast affect who can read and understand an artistic message?
vocab: Baseline
The line upon which most letters appear to rest in a line of text.
X-height
The height of typical lowercase letters, excluding ascenders and descenders.
Counter
The enclosed or partially enclosed space inside a letter, such as the interior of o or e.
Kerning
Adjustment of space between a particular pair of letterforms.
Tracking
Adjustment of overall letter spacing across a selected run of text.
Hierarchy
Visual ordering that helps readers identify a headline, subtitle, body and supporting details.
Legibility
Ease of distinguishing individual letterforms; separate from how comfortable a long passage is to read.

worked.intro: A tiny poster announces 'ART TODAY 4 PM' using ornate script throughout. At a distance the lettering merges and the event time disappears.
steps: Sketch two display headlines using original letterforms. In version A use tight spacing; in version B open the counters and increase the spacing between 'R' and 'T'.
Set the date and location in simpler letters with strong contrast. Compare at 30 cm and across a room, recording which words can be read without guessing.
Place the event time directly below the main title, then reduce decorative flourishes behind critical information.
Photograph the before and after, annotate baseline, counters, kerning pairs and a legibility test that includes an alternative high-contrast layout.

stages: Observe: Collect three examples of public lettering from permitted environments. Describe which letters are hardest to distinguish and the relationship among title, date and small print.

Research: Study two credited design examples from a museum or archive. Record designer or creator if known, publication context, accessible text alternatives and the purpose of each typographic choice.
Experiment: Draw at least eight original letters, compare thick/thin strokes, test two kerning pairs and try the same message at three sizes and two contrast levels.
Create and revise: Design a poster for a fictional exhibition; test reading distance with a volunteer or self-test and revise title, hierarchy and small-print contrast.
Reflect and archive: Present the letter studies, two poster states, explicit readability observations and source citations; distinguish a decorative artistic decision from an accessibility barrier.
lessons.assignment: Deliver an original 8-letter study, two contrasting headline experiments, a poster with clear event hierarchy, a documented reading-distance test with at least two readers or equivalent self-tests, and two annotated revisions.
lessons.alternative: Use pencil, ruler and gridded paper; no fonts, tablets or design software are required. Test a larger-font printout for accessibility.
lessons.ethics: Do not reproduce a typeface specimen or logo as your own original mark; credit admired designers and avoid publishing contact details for imagined events.
questions: What does a baseline help align?
Letters along a common writing line
The relative cost of ink
Which feature is an enclosed interior of a letter?
A counter
A caption
Why examine x-height?
It affects how lowercase letterforms appear at a given size
It determines the price of the poster
What does kerning adjust?
Spacing between a particular pair of letters
The hue of every printed letter
What does tracking adjust?
Letter spacing over a longer run of text
The paper's physical thickness
Which is an example of visual hierarchy?
Headline most prominent, with clear date and small supporting credit
All words made equally ornate
What does legibility mean?
Individual letters can be distinguished accurately
A letter has a historical origin
What may make an ornate script difficult to read?
Closed counters and confusing adjacent strokes
The number of letters in a word alone
How can one test a poster for distance readability?
Try several viewing distances and note errors
Assume the designer can read everything
Why provide sufficient text/background contrast?
Readers must be able to separate letters from their surroundings
Contrast proves the design is original
What should a title study include?
Different spacing and stroke treatments with observed results
Only the artist's favorite iteration
What is a useful typographic revision?
Open ambiguous letter shapes and separate critical details
Hide the time inside decoration
What belongs in a design reference citation?
Designer or source, title/context, date if known and URL
Only a vague claim that the font is famous
What can a simple pencil-based lettering exercise teach?
Letter shape, spacing and hierarchy without software
Only the technical settings of a printer
What distinguishes readability from decoration?
A design can be ornamental yet still must communicate essential words
Any decorative element is automatically inaccessible

lessons.title: Layout, Grids and Visual Systems
lessons.essential: How can an intentional grid improve coherence while leaving room for visual exploration and different reading paths?
vocab: Grid
An underlying system of rows, columns and alignments organizing a page.
Margin
A boundary of white space around the content.
Gutter
Space between columns or panels that prevents visual crowding.
Alignment
A repeated edge or axis that visually relates separate elements.
Negative space
Areas without visual content that separate, frame or emphasize information.
Modularity
Using repeated component sizes or patterns to form a coherent system.
Reading path
The order in which a reader is likely to inspect parts of a design.

worked.intro: A one-page community art guide contains a map, three event summaries and a phone-free contact method, but its irregular cards make the reading order ambiguous.
steps: Draw a three-column grid with equal gutters and comfortable margins; label the intended reader's first, second and third tasks.
Place one headline across all columns and three event modules below. Keep shared dates aligned and avoid placing essential labels outside the reader's field of view.
Create a second layout using only two columns. Compare scanning time, density and order using a simple comprehension task.
Revise whichever version has fewer errors and document the grid, modules, margin choices and accessibility fallback as a linear reading order.

stages: Observe: Examine three published informational layouts and mark their grid, margins, gutters, dominant headline, text blocks and image placement. Ask what a reader discovers first.
Research: Compare one contemporary design example and one historic poster from credited museum or library collections; record how audience, paper size and reproduction influenced the layout.
Experiment: Produce 2-, 3- and 4-column thumbnails of the same factual content. Change only the grid while keeping type sizes and words consistent; note tradeoffs.
Create and revise: Design a one-page fictional community arts guide with a headline, three modules, illustrations and a plainly labeled access note. Collect feedback using one find-the-time task.
Reflect and archive: Present grid overlays, alternatives, a corrected final layout and a paragraph explaining whether the grid helped readers or merely made the page look orderly.
lessons.assignment: Create three gridded thumbnail systems and one polished informational page, preserving exactly the same content across versions. Document at least one reading-path failure and an evidence-based revision.
lessons.alternative: Build layouts using folded paper, rectangles, cut-out headings and taped modules. Photograph each arrangement before glue is applied.
lessons.ethics: Avoid describing a fictional organization as real; keep important information available in linear text as well as decorative layouts.
questions: What does a design grid organize?
Repeated rows, columns and alignments
The artist's drawing medium alone
What is a gutter?
Space between content columns or panels
A panel's main title
What are margins?
White-space boundaries around page content
Random gaps inside letters
Why use consistent alignment?
It visually connects related content
It removes every creative choice
How does negative space help?
It separates and emphasizes information
It requires content to disappear entirely
What is a module in information design?
A repeatable content component within a system
Any unsourced artwork
What does reading path describe?
Likely order of visual attention across a page
The physical walk to a museum
Why compare two-column and three-column versions?
Different grids can change scan effort and available space
One grid is always correct in every medium
What is a fair layout test?
Keep message content constant while varying organization
Change every word and the grid at once
What should a grid overlay reveal?
Column edges and element alignment decisions
The personality of all readers
Which design choice reduces dense crowding?
Allow adequate gutters and margins
Pack unrelated facts into every empty corner
What is a useful comprehension task?
Ask a reader to find the event time
Ask the reader if they like the color
Why document a failed draft?
It explains the reason for a subsequent design revision
It invalidates all finished artwork
Which layout is most accessible as a fallback?
A meaningful linear reading order with the same facts
A page with only decorative icons
What can modularity provide?
Consistent repeated components across a page
A guarantee of historical accuracy

lessons.title: Information Design and Ethical Claims
lessons.essential: How can a visual explanation represent measured quantities, sources and uncertainty without distorting what is known?
vocab: Infographic
A visual arrangement of information combining text and graphical representations.
Scale
The relationship between a visual measure and the data value it represents.
Baseline
A defined reference value, such as zero in many bar charts.
Denominator
The total number or population to which a fraction or rate refers.
Uncertainty
A stated limit in precision, confidence or completeness of available evidence.
Source label
A citation that allows a viewer to trace where a figure or claim came from.
Pictogram
A repeated symbolic image used to represent a quantity or classification.

worked.intro: An art-club infographic reports 18 out of 30 survey respondents prefer morning workshops. A careless icon chart shows 18 icons beside only 10 for afternoon, even though twelve respondents preferred other times.
steps: Verify that the total sample is 30 and write a source line: 'Fictional classroom example: 18 of 30 respondents, 60%'. Avoid implying a whole city or school was surveyed.
Draw a bar from a clear zero baseline with values 18 and 12; label the denominator and categories. For a pictogram, make every icon equal one respondent and show thirty icons in total.
Create a misleading comparison by cropping the bar baseline, then correct it and explain the difference in perceived effect without implying a real finding.
Present the graph together with a plain-language summary, sample size, method limitations and a question inviting viewers to request the underlying data.

stages: Observe: Analyze two public charts, separating the plotted quantities from rhetoric. Check axes, labels, visual units, percentages and whether important categories are omitted.
Research: Locate one sourced public dataset or use an explicitly fictional class sample. Record original publication, sample definition, collection date and usage rights. Do not invent precision.
Experiment: Represent the same numbers as a labeled bar chart, a pictogram and a short plain-text table. Compare how quickly each format communicates totals and uncertainty.

Create and revise: Build a one-page infographic for an art supply inventory or simulated community survey. Run a reader test asking which group is largest, what the denominator is and how uncertain the claim is.
Reflect and archive: Keep the raw numbers, chart drafts, source ledger, revision notes and a final statement separating directly supported claims from speculation.
lessons.assignment: Design a source-labeled infographic with at least two graphical forms, a data table, clear denominator, true zero scale where appropriate, a limitations note and an audience comprehension test with documented revisions.
lessons.alternative: Use graph paper, repeated paper-square pictograms and handwritten labels. Use an invented dataset clearly labeled 'synthetic classroom example'.
lessons.ethics: Avoid unsupported statistics and manipulative area scaling. Cite all actual data and provide numerical text alongside graphics for accessibility.
questions: What does a chart denominator indicate?
The full group used to calculate a proportion
The color of the chart background
Why should bar charts often start at zero?
To avoid exaggerating differences in bar lengths
To guarantee all data are accurate
What does a source label let a reader do?
Trace the origin of a claim or number
Determine how famous the designer is
What is a pictogram?
A repeated symbol representing a count or category
A hidden signature in a photograph
Why identify a survey sample size?
It limits how widely results may reasonably be generalized
It changes the artwork's paper size
What is uncertainty?
A limit on precision, confidence or completeness of evidence
A missing decorative border
Which display is easiest to audit numerically?
A clear table listing values and totals
An unlabeled gradient
What makes a source-based infographic ethical?
Accurate measures, citations and explicit limitations
Beautiful colors without data checks
Why is an unlabeled truncated y-axis risky?
It may visually inflate small differences
It eliminates every relationship among values
What should synthetic practice data be called?
A clearly identified fictional classroom dataset
An official citywide survey
Why keep raw values with a graph?
They let viewers verify the graphical encoding
They hide which data were omitted
What is a useful reader test?
Ask what a figure shows, its total and its uncertainties
Ask whether viewers like the designer
What is a scale?
A rule mapping data values to visual units
A list of famous art movements
What makes an icon chart misleading?
Unequal icon sizes or inconsistent units for comparable counts
Using an icon to represent a value
How can accessibility improve an infographic?
Provide descriptive text and explicit values, not color alone
Hide all numbers from readers
